en: Thus have I heard— Dīgha Nikāya 33, the Saṅgītisutta.
On one occasion, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a large community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, the Blessed One arrived at Pāvā, a city of the Mallas.
There, the Blessed One stayed in Pāvā in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.
Now at that time, the Mallas of Pāvā had recently constructed a new assembly hall called Ubbhaṭaka; it had not yet been inhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being whatsoever.

The Mallas of Pāvā heard: “It is said that the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, has arrived at Pāvā and is staying at Pāvā in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.

Then the Mallas of Pāvā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Mallas of Pāvā said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here there is a new assembly hall of the Mallas of Pāvā called Ubbhaṭaka, recently built and not yet inhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One be the first to use it; once it has been used by the Blessed One, the Mallas of Pāvā will use it afterwards.
That would be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the Mallas of Pāvā.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then the Mallas of Pāvā, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, they approached the assembly hall; having arrived, they spread it all over with rugs.
Having spread the assembly hall, prepared seats for the Blessed One, set out a water vessel, and lit an oil lamp,
they approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those Mallas of Pāvā said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the assembly hall has been completely strewn with carpets; seats have been prepared for the Blessed One; a water jar has been set out; and an oil lamp has been raised.
Now, venerable sir, may the Blessed One do as he deems it the right time.”
Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the assembly hall together with the community of monks.
Having arrived, he washed his feet, entered the assembly hall,
and sat down leaning against the central pillar, facing the east.
The community of bhikkhus, having washed their feet, entered the assembly hall and sat down against the western wall facing east, with the Blessed One before them.
The Mallas of Pāvā, having washed their feet, entered the assembly hall and sat down against the eastern wall facing west, with the Blessed One before them.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Mallas of Pāvā for much of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma, dismissed them, saying:
"The night has passed, Vāseṭṭhas;
now you may do as you see fit."
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Mallas of Pāvā replied to the Blessed One. Having risen from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and departed.
Then, not long after the Mallas of Pāvā had left, the Blessed One surveyed the silent community of monks and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, the community of monks is free from sloth and torpor.”
“Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Sāriputta, for the bhikkhus.
My back aches;
I shall stretch it.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having folded his outer robe into four layers, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, with his mind fixed on the thought of rising.
Now at that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had recently passed away in Pāvā.
With his passing away, the Nigaṇṭhas split into two factions; they became contentious, quarrelsome, and fell into disputes, living while piercing one another with verbal weapons:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya.
How could you understand this Dhamma and Vinaya? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. [What is] consistent..."
“Mine is consistent, yours is inconsistent. What should have been said first you said last; what should have been said last you said first.
Your position has been overturned, your argument has been refuted, and you are defeated. Go forth to save your argument, or provide an explanation if you are able.
Indeed, it seemed as if nothing but slaughter was taking place among the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nātaputta.
Even those lay disciples of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who wear white garments have become disillusioned with the Nigaṇṭhas,
followers of Nātaputta, disenchanted with them, and turned away from them— just as one would be toward a poorly proclaimed and poorly expounded Dhamma and Vinaya,
which is not conducive to liberation, does not lead to peace, was not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose foundations are shattered, and which offers no refuge.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has recently passed away at Pāvā.
With his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas have split and become divided... [as above] ...with their stupa broken and without a refuge."
For it is thus, friends, with a Dhamma and Discipline that is ill-proclaimed, ill-expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One.
But this Dhamma, friends, has been well-proclaimed and well-expounded by our Blessed One; it leads out, is conducive to peace, and has been proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.
In this regard, all should recite it together and not dispute, so that this holy life may endure for a long time.
That would endure for a long time, and it would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world,
and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. And what, friends,
is that Dhamma well-expounded and well-proclaimed by our Blessed One— leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One?
Wherein all should recite together and not dispute, so that this holy life may endure for a long time and remain stable—
for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit,
and happiness of gods and humans?
1. The Single Dhamma. "Friends, there is one Dhamma that has been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In regard to this, all should recite it together and not dispute, so that this holy life may endure for a long time."
That would endure for a long time; that would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
What is that one quality?
"All beings subsist by nutriment; all beings subsist by volitional formations.
This, friends, is that one Dhamma rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
In this matter, all must recite together and not dispute, so that this holy life may endure for a long time and remain stable;
that would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare,
and happiness of gods and humans.
2. Pairs:
"Friends, there are indeed two things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together and not dispute them, so that this holy life may endure for a long time."

This would endure for a long time; it would be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Which two?
Name-and-form;
ignorance and craving for existence;
the view of becoming and the view of non-becoming.
Lack of moral shame and lack of moral dread;
moral shame and moral dread;
stubbornness and association with evil friends.
Being easy to speak with and having virtuous friends;
skillfulness regarding offenses and skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses;
skillfulness regarding meditative attainments and skillfulness regarding the emergence from meditative attainments.
Skillfulness regarding the elements and skillfulness regarding attention;
skillfulness regarding the sense bases and skillfulness regarding dependent origination;
skillfulness regarding what is possible and skillfulness regarding what is impossible.
Uprightness and modesty;
patience and gentleness; kindness and hospitality.
Non-violence and purity;
forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension;
mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties and lack of moderation in eating;
guarding the doors of the sense faculties and moderation in eating;
the power of reflection and the power of cultivation.
The power of mindfulness and the power of concentration; serenity and insight;
the sign of serenity and the sign of exertion.
Exertion and non-distraction;
failure in virtue and failure in view;
perfection in virtue and perfection in view.
Purification of virtue and purification of view.
Now, purification of view is the striving of one who has seen [the truth].
A sense of urgency regarding things that should inspire urgency, and systematic striving by one who is stirred with urgency.
Discontent with regard to wholesome states and non-receding in the face of effort;
clear knowledge and liberation;
the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
"Friends, these two things have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding them, all should recite together and not dispute, so that this holy life may endure for a long time and remain stable;
that would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit [of devas and humans]."
For the welfare and happiness of gods and humans. 3.
The Triads:
"Friends, there are indeed three things that have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, who is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha."
In this regard, all should recite together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
What are the three?
The three unwholesome roots: [greed, hatred, and delusion].
Greed is a root of unwholesomeness, hatred is a root of unwholesomeness, and delusion is a root of unwholesomeness.
There are three roots of wholesomeness:
non-greed is a root of wholesomeness, non-hatred is a root of wholesomeness, and non-delusion is a root of wholesomeness.
Three types of misconduct:
bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Three types of good conduct: [bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct].
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
Three unwholesome thoughts:
sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought.
Three wholesome thoughts:
the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
Three unwholesome intentions:
The thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty.
The three wholesome thoughts:
the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
Three unwholesome perceptions:
the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty.
Three wholesome perceptions:
The perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-cruelty.
The three unwholesome elements:
the element of sensuality, the element of ill will, and the element of cruelty.
Three wholesome elements:
the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-cruelty.
Furthermore, there are three other elements:
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Another three realms:
the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation.
There are another three elements:
the inferior element, the middling element, and the superior element.
There are three kinds of craving:
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Furthermore, there are three other kinds of craving:
craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
There are also three other kinds of craving:
craving for form, craving for the formless, and craving for cessation.
There are three fetters:
The view of a personal body, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
The three taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
There are three kinds of existence:
existence in the sense-sphere, existence in the form-sphere, and existence in the formless-sphere.
There are three kinds of seeking:
The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life.
The three conceits:
the conceit "I am superior," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior."
There are three times:
the past time, the future time, and the present time.
There are three ends:
Personal identity is an extreme; the origin of personal identity is an extreme; the cessation of personal identity is an extreme.
There are three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Three kinds of suffering:
the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change.
Three groups:
The group fixed in falsehood, the group fixed in truth, and the group that is undetermined.
There are three kinds of darkness:
regarding the past time, one hesitates, doubts, is not convinced, and does not have confidence; [regarding] the future...
Or he wavers, doubts, is not convinced, and does not have confidence regarding the past;
or he wavers, doubts, is not convinced, and does not have confidence regarding the present.
There are three things that the Tathāgata need not guard against:
"Friends, the Tathāgata is pure in bodily conduct; there is no misconduct of body on the part of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking:
'Lest another should find this out about me.
Friends, the Tathāgata is pure in verbal conduct; there is no misconduct of speech on the part of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard..."
‘Let no one else know this of me.
Friends, the Tathāgata is pure in mental conduct; there is no mental misconduct in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking:
‘Let no one else know this of me.’
There are three defilements:
lust is a defilement, hatred is a defilement, and delusion is a defilement.
There are three fires:
The fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
There are another three fires:
the fire of those worthy of offerings, the fire of the householder, and the fire of those worthy of alms.
The inclusion of form is threefold:
form that is visible and impinging, form that is invisible and impinging, and form that is invisible and non-impinging.
There are three formations:
The formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable.
Three types of persons:
the person in training, the person beyond training, and the person who is neither in training nor beyond training.
There are three kinds of elders:
the elder by birth, the elder by Dhamma, and the elder by convention.
There are three bases for meritorious action:
The basis for meritorious action consisting in giving, the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, and the basis for meritorious action consisting in meditation.
There are three grounds for censure:
by what is seen, by what is heard, and by suspicion.
There are three kinds of rebirth in the realm of sensual pleasure:

There are beings, friends, for whom sensual pleasures have appeared; they live under the sway of those sensual pleasures that have appeared, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first kind of rebirth in the realm of sensual pleasure.
There are, friends, beings who create their own sensual pleasures; having created them again and again, they exercise mastery over those sensual pleasures, just like the gods who Delight in Creation.
This is the second rebirth in the realm of sensual pleasure.

There are, friends, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures created by others; they exercise mastery over those sensual pleasures created by others, just like the gods who Wield Power over the Creations of Others.
This is the third mode of rebirth in the realm of sensual pleasure.
There are three modes of rebirth in happiness:
friends, there are beings who, having repeatedly generated [joy], dwell in happiness, such as the gods of the Brahma-body.
This is the first rebirth into happiness.
There are, friends, beings who are drenched, steeped, filled, and suffused with happiness.
From time to time they utter an inspired exclamation:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’—just like the Ābhassara devas.
This is the second rebirth in happiness.
There are beings, friends, who are drenched, steeped, filled, and suffused with happiness.
Being peaceful, they experience happiness just as the Subhakiṇha devas do.
This is the third rebirth in happiness.
There are three kinds of wisdom:
Wisdom of the trainee, wisdom of the adept, and wisdom that is neither of the trainee nor of the adept.
There are another three kinds of wisdom:
wisdom consisting in reflection, wisdom consisting in hearing, and wisdom consisting in cultivation.
Three weapons:
the weapon of learning, the weapon of seclusion, and the weapon of wisdom.
Three faculties:
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.
Three eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom.
The three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
The three developments:
The development of the body, the development of the mind, and the development of wisdom.
The three unsurpassed things:
the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed practice, and the unsurpassed liberation.
There are three kinds of concentration:

concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
There are another three kinds of concentration:
The emptiness concentration, the signless concentration, and the desireless concentration.
The three purities:
purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
The three types of nobility:
nobility of body, nobility of speech, and nobility of mind.
The three kinds of skill:
Skill in acquisition, skill in avoidance, and skill in means.
Three kinds of intoxication:
intoxication with health, intoxication with youth, and intoxication with life.
Three authorities:
authority over oneself, authority over the world, and authority over the Dhamma.
Three bases for discourse:
One might speak concerning the past time, saying:
"Thus it was in the past";
or one might speak concerning the future time, saying: [“Thus it will be in the future”].
‘It will be thus in the future time,’ or concerning the present time, one might speak thus:
‘It is thus now in the present time.’
The three true knowledges:

the knowledge of recollecting past lives is a true knowledge; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is a true knowledge; the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is a true knowledge.
The three abidings:
The divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.
The three marvels:
the marvel of psychic power, the marvel of mind-reading, and the marvel of instruction.
"Friends, these three things have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding them, all should recite together in harmony... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans. 4.
The Tetrad (Catukka)
"Friends, there are indeed four teachings rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together and not dispute them... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
What are the four?"
The four foundations of mindfulness.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … [and so on] … *Note: The ellipsis indicates the repetition of the formula for the remaining foundations of mindfulness:
contemplating mind in mind and mental phenomena in mental phenomena.*

He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
The four right strivings.
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states."

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
These are the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
Here, friends, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
The four jhānas.

Here, friends, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness," and thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
There are four developments of concentration.
There is, friends, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
There is, friends, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.
"Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints.
And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life?"
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,
enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna... [pe] ...the fourth jhāna.
"Friends, this development of concentration, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu attends to the perception of light, he fixes his mind on the perception of day: as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day."
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.
This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.
And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension?
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu’s feelings arise known, they persist known, and they subside known.
His perceptions arise known, they persist known, and they subside known.
His thoughts arise known, they persist known, and they subside known."
"Friends, this development of concentration, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging."
Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away.
Such is feeling ... [and so on] ... such is perception ...
"Thus are volitional formations...
thus is consciousness, thus is the arising of consciousness, thus is the passing away of consciousness.
This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints."
The four immeasurables.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;

likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
He dwells pervading the world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion … [and so on] … with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy … [and so on] …
He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity. Likewise the second; likewise the third;

likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
The four formless attainments.

Here, friends, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Having completely surmounted the base of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The four supports.

In this case, friends, a bhikkhu, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures another; having reflected, he avoids another; having reflected, he dispels another. These are the four noble lineages.
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is content with whatever robe he has; through contentment with whatever robe he has...
He speaks in praise of [contentment with] robes, yet he does not engage in improper search for the sake of robes;
not obtaining robes, he does not become anxious, and having obtained robes, he uses them without attachment, infatuation, or obsession, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape;
moreover, by means of that contentment with whatever robe he may have, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, he, friends, is called a bhikkhu who stands firm in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of almsfood whatsoever;
he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood, and he does not, for the sake of almsfood, engage in improper or unsuitable search; and even when he does not obtain almsfood...
He does not become anxious; and having obtained almsfood, he consumes it without being attached, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger in it and understanding the escape from it.
Furthermore, by means of that contentment with whatever almsfood is received, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—that person, friends, is said to be “a bhikkhu established in the ancient, primordial lineage of the noble ones.”
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of lodging at all, and he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of lodging.
He does not resort to improper means for the sake of a lodging, nor is he anxious when he does not obtain one.
When he obtains a lodging, he is not infatuated, not intoxicated, and not obsessed by it; he sees the danger in it.
He uses them with wisdom regarding escape; and by means of that contentment with any kind of lodging, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—this, friends, is called a monk who stands firm in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
Furthermore, friends, a monk delights in relinquishing and rejoices in relinquishing; he delights in mental development and rejoices in mental development.
And by means of that delight in abandoning, that joy in abandoning, that delight in cultivation, and that joy in cultivation, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—this, friends, is called a bhikkhu who stands firm in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
These are the four strivings.
The effort of restraint, the effort of abandoning, the effort of development, and the effort of protection.
And what, friends, is the effort of restraint?
Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— might flow in upon him,
he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of the eye, and attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one were to dwell with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in, one practices for its restraint;
one guards the faculty of mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
This, friends, is called the effort of restraint.
And what, friends, is the effort of abandoning?
Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence.
He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will...
an arisen thought of cruelty...
nor does he tolerate whatever evil, unwholesome states that arise; he abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence.
This, friends, is called the effort of abandoning.
And what, friends, is the effort of development?
Here, monks, a monk develops the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … he develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture …
He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility… he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
This, friends, is called the effort for development.
And what, friends, is the effort for preservation?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu preserves a favorable sign of concentration that has arisen—namely, the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, and the perception of a bloated corpse.
This, friends, is called the effort of preservation.
There are four kinds of knowledge:
knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of inference, knowledge of penetration, and knowledge of conventional designation.
There are also four other kinds of knowledge:
knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
There are four factors of stream-entry:
Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—
these are the four factors of a stream-enterer.
Here, friends, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.’
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically;
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing correctly—namely, the four pairs of persons.”

‘There are eight types of persons; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unsullied, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
The four fruits of asceticism:
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship.
The four elements:
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
The four nutriments:
physical nutriment, whether gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.
There are four stations of consciousness.
Friend, when consciousness stands supported by form, having form as its object and established upon form, it comes to growth, increase, and abundance, being moistened by delight.
Or, friend, [when consciousness stands supported] by feeling...
Or, friend, consciousness, when it persists, persists by means of perception...

or, friend, consciousness, when it persists, persists by means of volitional formations; having volitional formations as its object and being established upon volitional formations, it reaches growth, increase, and abundance, being moistened by delight.
There are four ways of going to ruin:
He goes astray through desire, he goes astray through hatred, he goes astray through delusion, and he goes astray through fear.
There are four origins of craving:
friend, craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of robes; [likewise on account of almsfood, lodgings, and for the sake of the life of a recluse].
"Friends, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of almsfood; craving arises in a bhikkhu because of lodgings;
or craving arises in a bhikkhu because of the pursuit of this or that state of existence."
There are four modes of practice:

practice that is painful with slow direct knowledge, practice that is painful with quick direct knowledge, practice that is pleasant with slow direct knowledge, and practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge.
There are another four modes of practice:
The practice of forbearance, the practice of patience, the practice of self-mastery, and the practice of equanimity.
The four footprints of the Dhamma:
non-covetousness is a footprint of the Dhamma; non-ill will is a footprint of the Dhamma; right mindfulness is a footprint of the Dhamma; and right concentration is a footprint of the Dhamma.
There are four ways of undertaking things.
There is, friends, a way of undertaking things that is painful in the present and results in pain in the future.
There is, friends, a way of undertaking things that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future.
Friends, there is an undertaking of things that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future.
Friends, there is an undertaking of things that is pleasant both in the present and results in happiness in the future.
There are four aggregates of Dhamma:
The aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, and the aggregate of liberation.
The four powers:
the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
The four foundations:
the foundation of wisdom, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, and the foundation of peace.
The four ways of answering questions:
A question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered with a counter-question, a question to be answered by analysis, and a question to be set aside.
There are four types of formal acts (kamma):
There is, friends, a formal act that is dark with dark result.
"Friends, there is action that is bright with a bright result.
Friends, there is action that is dark with a dark result.
Friends, there is action that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, which leads to the destruction of action."
There are four things to be realized:
past lives are to be realized through mindfulness;
the passing away and rebirth of beings is to be realized through the eye.
The eight liberations are to be realized by means of the body;
the destruction of the taints is to be realized by means of wisdom.
The four floods—
The flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
The four yokes:
the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
Four disengagements:
disengagement from the bond of sensual desire, disengagement from the bond of existence, disengagement from the bond of views, and disengagement from the bond of ignorance.
Four ties:
Covetousness is a bodily tie; ill will is a bodily tie; adherence to rules and observances is a bodily tie; dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth" is a bodily tie.
There are four kinds of clinging:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
There are four modes of birth:
birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and spontaneous birth.
There are four ways of entering the womb.

"Here, friends, a certain person enters the mother’s womb without full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness; this is the first descent into the womb.

Furthermore, friends, here a certain person enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness; this is the second descent into the womb."

Furthermore, friends, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness, but emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness; this is the third descent into the womb.

Furthermore, friends, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb with full awareness; this is the fourth descent into the womb.
These are the four acquisitions of an individual existence.
Friends, there is an acquisition of a personal existence in which one’s own volition alone operates, not the volition of another.
Friends, there is an acquisition of a personal existence in which the volition of another alone operates, not one’s own volition.
Friends, there is an acquisition of a personal existence in which both one’s own volition and the volition of another operate.
"Friends, there are eight acquisitions of an individual existence, in which neither one's own volition nor another's volition operates.
There are four purifications of offerings.
Friends, there is an offering that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient."
"Friends, there is a gift that is purified by the recipient, not by the donor.
Friends, there is a gift that is purified neither by the donor nor by the recipient.
Friends, there is a gift that is purified both by the donor and by the recipient."
The four bases of sympathy:
generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
The four ignoble modes of speech:
False speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
The four noble modes of expression:
abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter.
Furthermore, there are four ignoble modes of speech:
claiming to have seen what was not seen, claiming to have heard what was not heard, claiming to have sensed what was not sensed, and claiming to have cognized what was not cognized.
Furthermore, there are four noble modes of speech: [the opposite of each of the above].
To say one has not seen what was not seen, to say one has not heard what was not heard, to say one has not sensed what was not sensed, and to say one has not cognized what was not cognized.
Furthermore, there are four other ignoble modes of speech:
to say one has seen what was seen, to say one has heard what was heard, to say one has sensed what was sensed, and to say one has cognized what was cognized.
There are also four noble modes of speech:

speaking of what was seen as having been seen, speaking of what was heard as having been heard, speaking of what was sensed as having been sensed, and speaking of what was cognized as having been cognized.
There are four types of persons.
"Here, friends, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-tormenting.
Here, friends, a certain person torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Here, friends, a certain person both torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-tormenting, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others."
"Here, friends, a certain person does not torment himself nor is he devoted to the practice of self-torment; he does not torment others nor is he devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Without tormenting himself or others, he dwells in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, with a self that has become sublime.
There are also four other types of persons."
"Here, friends, one kind of person practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others.
Here, friends, another kind of person practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit.
Here, friends, yet another kind of person practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others."
"Here, friends, a certain person practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.
There are four other types of persons:
one who goes from darkness to darkness, one who goes from darkness to light, one who goes from light to darkness, and one who goes from light to light."
There are also four other types of persons:
the ascetic who is immovable, the ascetic who is a red lotus, the ascetic who is a white lotus, and the ascetic who is a delicate jasmine among ascetics.
These, friends, are the four things rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One, the knower, the seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In this regard, all must recite it together in unison... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
The first section for recitation is finished.
5. The Pentads.
"Friends, there are five things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together in harmony... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
What are the five?"
The five aggregates:
the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
The five aggregates of clinging.

The aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
The five strands of sensual pleasure:
forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
Sounds cognizable by the ear...
odors cognizable by the nose...
flavors cognizable by the tongue...
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
The five destinations:
hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, human beings, and devas.
The five kinds of stinginess:
stinginess regarding dwelling, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.
The five hindrances:
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
The five lower fetters:
personality view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.
The five higher fetters:
lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
The five training rules:

Abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors that are the basis for negligence.
There are five impossible things.
Friends, it is impossible for a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints to intentionally deprive a living being of life. It is impossible for one who has destroyed the taints...
A bhikkhu is incapable of taking what is not given, which is reckoned as theft. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding, just as he did formerly when he was a householder.
There are five calamities:
the calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of disease, the calamity of moral failure, and the calamity of wrong view.

Friends, it is not on account of the calamity of relatives, nor the calamity of wealth, nor the calamity of disease that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Friends, it is on account of the ruin of virtue or the ruin of view that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, or hell.
There are five accomplishments:
accomplishment in kinsmen, accomplishment in wealth, accomplishment in health, accomplishment in virtue, and accomplishment in view.

Friends, it is not because of success in kinsmen, or success in wealth, or success in health that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Rather, friends, it is because of success in virtue or success in view that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
There are five dangers for one who is immoral due to the failure of virtue.
"Here, friends, an immoral person, one who has failed in virtue, through negligence incurs a great loss of wealth;
this is the first danger for an immoral person who has failed in virtue.
Furthermore, friends, an evil reputation spreads concerning an immoral person who has failed in virtue."
This is the second danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, friends, whatever assembly an immoral person who has failed in virtue approaches—
whether an assembly of kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, or ascetics— they approach it lacking confidence and feeling abashed.
This is the third danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, friends, an immoral person who has failed in virtue dies confused;
this is the fourth danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, friends, an immoral person who has failed in virtue, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell;
this is the fifth danger for the immoral person due to their failure in virtue.
There are five benefits for one who is virtuous due to their perfection of virtue.
"Here, friends, one who is virtuous and perfect in virtue acquires a great mass of wealth through diligence;
this is the first benefit for one who is virtuous in their perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, friends, a good reputation arises for one who is virtuous and perfect in virtue."
This is the second benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, friends, whatever assembly a virtuous person endowed with virtue approaches—
whether an assembly of kshatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics— they approach it confident and self-assured.
This is the third benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, friends, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue dies unconfused;
this is the fourth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, friends, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world;
this is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
When a monk wishes to reprove another, friends, he should reprove that person after establishing five qualities within himself.
I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time;
I shall speak what is true, not what is untrue;
I shall speak gently, not harshly.
"I shall speak for what is connected with the goal, not for what is unconnected with the goal;
I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of ill will.
Friend, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reprove that person after having established these five qualities within himself.
The five factors of striving.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
He is free from illness and affliction, endowed with a digestive capacity that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for exertion.
He is honest and sincere, revealing himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; steadfast, firm in effort, and not relinquishing his burden regarding wholesome qualities.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
There are five Pure Abodes:
the Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha.
There are five types of non-returners:

one who attains nibbāna in the interval, one who attains nibbāna upon landing, one who attains nibbāna without exertion, one who attains nibbāna with exertion, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
There are five mental barrennesses.
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher.

For that bhikkhu who is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving; and since his mind does not so incline..."
“Exertion, application, persistence, and striving— this is the first wilderness of the mind.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is doubtful and uncertain about the Dhamma … he is doubtful and uncertain about the Saṅgha …”
He is doubtful and uncertain about the training...
he is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, harboring a grudge.
That monk, friends, who is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, harboring a grudge—

His mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving; for one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this is the fifth mental barrenness.
There are five mental shackles.

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he has not abandoned desire for them, has not abandoned affection for them, has not abandoned thirst for them, has not abandoned fever for them, and has not abandoned craving for them.

For that bhikkhu who is not free from lust for sensual pleasures—who has not abandoned desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for them—his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
And when his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving..."
This is the first mental bond.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not free from lust for the body … [and so on] … he is not free from lust for forms … [and so on].
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu eats as much as he likes until his belly is full, and dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness...

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas, thinking: "By this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or one among the devas.
That bhikkhu, friends, who leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas, thinking: "By this..."
‘By means of virtue, or vows, or asceticism, or the holy life, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity’—
his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving. For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor,
devotion, perseverance, and striving...
This is the fifth mental bond.
There are five faculties:
the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty.
There are another five faculties:
the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
There are yet another five faculties:
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
There are five elements of escape.

Here, friends, when a bhikkhu directs his attention to sensual pleasures, his mind does not leap forward toward them, does not find confidence in them, does not settle upon them, and is not liberated from them.
But when he attends to renunciation, his mind leaps forward into renunciation, becomes serene, settles, and is liberated.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from sensual desires.
And as for those taints, vexations, and fevers that arise conditioned by sensual desires—he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from sensual desires.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to ill will, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle down in it, and is not liberated by it.
But when he attends to non-ill will, his mind leaps forward toward it, finds confidence in it, settles down in it, and is liberated by it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from ill will.
Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by ill will—he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from ill will.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to cruelty, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not become settled in it, does not find stability in it, and is not liberated in it.
But when he attends to non-cruelty, his mind leaps forward toward it, becomes settled in it, finds stability in it, and is liberated in it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from cruelty.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by cruelty—one is freed from them; one does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from cruelty.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to forms, his mind does not leap forward toward them, does not find confidence in them, does not settle upon them, and is not liberated from them.
But when he attends to the formless, his mind leaps forward into the formless, becomes serene, settles, and is liberated.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from forms.
And whatever taints, vexations, or fevers arise conditioned by forms—from those he is freed; he does not experience that feeling.
This has been declared as the escape from forms.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to personal existence, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to the cessation of personal existence, his mind leaps forward toward the cessation of personal existence, finds confidence in it, settles upon it, and is liberated from it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from personal existence (sakkāya).
And as for those taints (āsava), distresses, and fevers that arise conditioned by personal existence—he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from personal existence.
There are five bases of liberation.
Here, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or some venerable companion in the holy life does so.
In whatever way the Teacher or that venerable companion in the holy life teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, in just that way he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.

For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises; for one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the first basis of liberation.

Furthermore, friends, it may be that neither the Teacher nor another venerable companion in the holy life teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu; yet he himself teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and mastered it... [and so on]... This is the second basis of liberation.
Furthermore, he recites in detail the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it...
Furthermore, he reflects upon and examines with his mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it, scrutinizing it with his intellect...
Furthermore, he has correctly grasped a certain object of concentration, attended to it well, retained it well, and penetrated it well with wisdom.
To whatever extent, friends, a bhikkhu has properly grasped, attended to, well retained,
and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom a particular object of concentration, to that same extent he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.

For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises; in one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
This is the fifth basis for liberation. There are five perceptions that ripen liberation:

The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of relinquishment, and the perception of dispassion.
These, friends, are the five things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
6. The Sixfold Set:
"Friends, there are six things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In regard to these, all should recite them together... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans."
Which six?
The six internal sense bases:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
The six external sense bases:
the base of visible forms, the base of sounds, the base of odors, the base of tastes, the base of tangibles, and the base of mental phenomena.
The six classes of consciousness:
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
The six groups of contact:
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
Six classes of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
Six classes of perception:
Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, perception of mental phenomena.
Six classes of volition:
volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, volition regarding odors, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding tangibles, volition regarding mental phenomena.
Six groups of craving:
craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
Six kinds of disrespect.
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher; he dwells without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma;
he dwells without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha; he dwells without reverence and deference toward the training;
he dwells without reverence and deference toward heedfulness; and he dwells without reverence and deference toward hospitality.
The six respects.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with respect and deference toward the Teacher; he dwells with respect and deference toward the Dhamma;
he dwells with respect and deference toward the Saṅgha; he dwells with respect and deference toward the training.
He dwells with reverence for and deference toward heedfulness; he dwells with reverence for and deference toward hospitality.
There are six modes of mental exploration accompanied by joy:
having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for joy.
There are six explorations of displeasure.
Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for mental distress ... [and so on] ...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one dwells upon a mental phenomenon that is a basis for mental distress.
There are six modes of dwelling upon equanimity.

Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for equanimity …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a mental phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity.
The six principles of cordiality.
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu maintains bodily acts of loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private.
This quality is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu maintains verbal acts of loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private."
This quality, too, is memorable... it leads to unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable... it leads to unity.

Furthermore, friends, whatever gains are righteous and righteously obtained—even if only as much as is contained in a single alms-bowl—a bhikkhu shares such gains with his virtuous companions in the holy life, not hoarding them for himself.
This quality, too, is conducive to harmony... it leads to unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells possessing in common with his companions in the holy life those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating,
praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration—
both openly and in private.
This, too, is a principle that is memorable... [it leads] to unity.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells both in public and in private possessing in common with his companions in the holy life that view which is noble, leading out, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering; he dwells in such a view shared in common with them.
This, too, is a principle that is memorable, which creates affection, creates respect, and leads to gathering together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
There are six roots of dispute.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is angry and resentful.
That bhikkhu who is angry and resentful dwells without respect and without deference even toward the Teacher.
He dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Dhamma; he dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Saṅgha;
he does not fulfill the training.
That monk, friends, who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, and dwells disrespectful toward the Dhamma...
Lacking respect, he dwells without reverence for the Saṅgha; lacking respect, he does not fulfill the training.
He creates a dispute within the Saṅgha—a dispute which is for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, and for the detriment, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.
Friends, if you should perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or among others, you should strive, friends, to abandon that very evil root of dispute.
If you do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, then, friends, you should practice so that this evil root of dispute does not flow forth in the future.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute; in this way, there is the non-outflow of this evil root of dispute in the future.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who slanders and is prone to resentment... [and so on].
He is envious and stingy … he is fraudulent and deceitful … he has evil desires and wrong view …
He is one who clings to his own views, is obstinate in his grasp, and is difficult to disabuse of them...
Friend, that bhikkhu who clings to his own views, is obstinate in his grasp, and is difficult to disabuse of them, dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher;
he dwells without respect and without deference toward the Dhamma; he dwells without respect toward the Saṅgha.
He dwells without deference and does not fulfill the training.
That monk, friends, who dwells without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher, who dwells without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma,
who dwells without reverence and without deference toward the Saṅgha, and who does not fulfill the training— he [is one] in the Saṅgha...
It gives rise to dispute. Such a dispute is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, and for the ruin, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.
If, friends, you should perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or externally, then, friends, you should strive for the abandoning of that very evil root of dispute.

If you, friends, do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, then, friends, you should practice for the sake of the future non-outflow of that very same evil root of dispute.
In this way, there is the abandoning of that evil root of dispute; in this way, there is the future non-outflow of that evil root of dispute.
The six elements:
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
These are the six elements that lead to escape.
In this regard, friends, a bhikkhu might say:
‘Indeed, my liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken;
yet ill will still persists, seizing hold of my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable Sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One would not speak thus.’

"It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen, that when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, ill will should still take possession of the mind; such a thing is not possible.
For this, friend, is the escape from ill will: namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness."
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:
"Indeed, I have developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a foundation of, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the liberation of mind through compassion;
yet nevertheless, cruelty still persists, obsessing my mind."
He should be told: "Do not say this, friend; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the liberation of mind through compassion has been developed, cultivated, made much of, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, yet ill will should still take possession of the mind—such a thing is not possible."
"For this, friend, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion.
Furthermore, friend, here a bhikkhu might say:
"Indeed, by me the liberation of mind through gladness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken."
‘And yet discontent still persists, obsessing my mind,’ he should be told:
‘Do not say so, Venerable One; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, nor would the Blessed One ever speak thus.

It is impossible, friend, it is out of the question, that when the liberation of the mind through sympathetic joy has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, [discontent should persist].’”
"Yet it is impossible that discontent should persist by taking possession of his mind;
for there is an escape from discontent, friend, namely, the liberation of the mind through sympathetic joy.
Then, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:

‘Although equanimity as liberation of mind has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken by me, yet passion still persists, seizing my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable Sir; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.’

"It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen, that when the liberation of mind through equanimity has been developed, cultivated, made the vehicle, made the foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, passion should still persist by obsessing the mind—such a case does not exist.
For this, friend, is the escape from passion: namely, the liberation of mind through equanimity."
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:
"Indeed, my signless liberation of mind has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken by me.
And yet, my consciousness still follows after signs."
Thus one should say to him: "Do not speak thus, friend; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.

Friend, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that consciousness should still follow after signs in one whose mind-release through the signless has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken."
"For this, friends, is the escape from all signs, namely, the signless liberation of mind.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say here:
"The thought 'I am' has vanished for me; I do not perceive 'this I am'."
‘And yet, this arrow of doubt and perplexity still remains, obsessing my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, friend; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that while the notion “I am” has vanished and one no longer perceives “I am this,” the arrow of doubt and perplexity should remain obsessing the mind.’”
"Yet it is impossible that the arrow of doubt and perplexity should persist, taking possession of his mind;
for this, friends, is the escape from the arrow of doubt and perplexity, namely, the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'.
The six unsurpassed things:
The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection.
The six bases for recollection:
recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities.
There are six constant abidings.
Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither glad nor sad; he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having cognized a phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
There are six classes of beings.
Here, friends, a certain person belonging to the dark class gives birth to a dark phenomenon.
"Furthermore, friends, here someone born of a dark class gives birth to a bright state.
Furthermore, friends, here someone born of a dark class gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright.
Furthermore, friends, here someone born of a bright class gives birth to a bright state."
"Furthermore, friends, here someone born of a bright class gives birth to dark states.
Furthermore, friends, here someone born of a bright class gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright.
There are six perceptions conducive to penetration."

The perception of impermanence regarding the impermanent, the perception of suffering regarding what is suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
These, friends, are the six things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
7. The Section on Sevenfold Teachings.
"Friends, there are seven teachings that have been rightly expounded by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together in harmony... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans."
Which seven?
The seven noble treasures:
the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom.
The seven factors of enlightenment:

the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
The seven requisites for concentration:
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Seven things contrary to the true Dhamma:
here, friends, a bhikkhu is without faith, shameless, reckless, of little learning, lazy, muddle-minded, and lacking wisdom.
Seven true qualities:
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, possessed of a sense of shame, possessed of moral dread, learned, energetic, established in mindfulness, and wise.
Seven qualities of a true person:
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is one who knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows moderation, knows the right time, knows the assembly, and knows individuals.
There are seven grounds for praise.
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu has intense desire for undertaking the training, and he does not lose his affection for undertaking the training in the future.
He has a keen desire for settling in the Dhamma, and his love for settling in the Dhamma remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for the removal of longing, and his love for the removal of longing remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for seclusion, and his love for seclusion remains undiminished in the future.
