He has an intense desire for the arousal of energy, and his love for the arousal of energy remains undiminished in the future.
He has an intense desire for mindfulness and discernment, and his love for mindfulness and discernment remains undiminished in the future.
He has an intense desire for the penetration of views, and his love for the penetration of views remains undiminished in the future.
Seven perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
Seven powers:
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
The seven stations of consciousness.
There are beings, friends, who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have been reborn there for the first time.
This is the second station of consciousness.
“There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara devas.
This is the third station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.”
This is the fourth station of consciousness.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
There are seven persons worthy of offerings:
one liberated both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a follower of Dhamma, and a follower of faith.
Seven underlying tendencies:

the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Seven fetters:
The fetters are: the fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of lust for existence, and the fetter of ignorance.

There are seven principles for settling legal issues—for the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise: the settlement in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) should be granted; the settlement by recollection (*sativinaya*)...

The act of confession (*dātabba*) should be granted, the verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) should be granted, a formal act based on admission (*paṭiññāya kāretabbaṃ*) should be carried out, the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*), the verdict for the worse (*tassapāpiyasikā*), and the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
These, friends, are the seven things rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
herein all should recite them together in harmony... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
The second recitation section is finished.
8. The Octad:
"Friends, there are eight things that have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
In this regard, all should recite together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
What are the eight?
The eight wrongnesses:
Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
The eight rightnesses:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Eight persons are worthy of offerings:
one who has entered the stream, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; one who returns once more, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
one who does not return, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; and an arahant, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship.
The eight bases of laziness.
Here, friends, a task must be done by a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
‘I have work to be done; while doing my work, my body will become weary; come now, let me lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the first ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has performed some work.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed performed work; while performing that work, my body is weary. Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy...
this is the second ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu must travel a road.
It occurs to him:
“I must travel along a road; as I travel along the road, my body will become weary. Come now, let me lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy.
This is the third ground for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has traveled along a road,
and it occurs to him:
‘I have indeed traveled along the road, and as I was traveling along the road, my body is weary; well now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy...
This is the fourth ground for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain as much coarse or refined food as he requires to satisfy him.
It occurs to him:
“While walking for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as required to satisfy me; my body is weary and unfit for work. Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy...
this is the fifth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or town, obtains as much as he needs and a full measure of food, whether coarse or refined.
It occurs to him:
“While wandering for alms in a village or town, I have received as much food as I needed, whether coarse or refined, to my full satisfaction;
my body is heavy and unwieldy, as if stuffed with fat. Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy… this is the sixth ground for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a slight illness has arisen in a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
“This slight ailment has arisen in me;
there is time for reclining, so let me lie down.”
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy… this is the seventh basis of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recently recovered from an illness and has not long been free from it.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed recovered from illness; it has not been long since I rose from my sickness, and my body is weak and unfit for work. Come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the eighth ground for laziness.
There are eight grounds for exertion.
Here, friends, a task must be done by a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
"I have work to be done; while performing that work, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized..."
‘for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the reaching of what has not been reached, for the realization of what has not been realized.
He arouses energy for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the reaching of what has not been reached, for the realization of what has not been realized.
This is the first basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has performed an action.
It occurs to him:
‘I have indeed performed an action; while performing that action, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ [as before]…
He arouses energy… this is the second basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu must travel along a road.
It occurs to him:
“I must travel along a road, and while traveling along that road, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Come now, I shall arouse energy... [as before]...
He arouses energy… this is the third basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has traveled along a road.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed traveled along the path; while traveling along the path, however, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, let me arouse energy...
... He arouses energy.
This is the fourth basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain as much coarse or refined food as he requires for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:

‘While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction; therefore, my body is light and fit for work. Come now, let me arouse energy.
… He arouses energy. … This is the fifth basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he obtains as much of coarse or refined food as he needs for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:

“I have indeed obtained as much of coarse or refined food as I needed for my full satisfaction while walking for alms in a village or town; my body is strong and fit for work. Come now, let me arouse energy... [and so on].
He arouses energy… this is the sixth basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a slight illness has arisen in a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
“This slight affliction has arisen in me; however, it is possible that this affliction might increase. Come now, let me arouse energy…” … [as before] … he arouses energy.
This is the seventh basis for undertaking [the training].
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recently recovered from an illness; he has not long been free from his sickness.
It occurs to him:
‘I have indeed recovered from my illness, having not long emerged from it;
yet it is possible that my affliction might recur. Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the witnessing of the unwitnessed.’
Thus one arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the actualization of the unactualized.
This is the eighth basis for exertion.
The eight bases for generosity.
One gives a gift out of resentment; one gives a gift out of fear; one gives a gift thinking, "He gave to me"; one gives a gift thinking, "He will give to me";
one gives a gift thinking, "Giving is good"; one gives a gift thinking, "I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not right for me, while cooking, not to give to those who do not cook";
and one gives a gift thinking, "As I give this gift, a fine reputation will spread about me."
One gives a gift for the purpose of adorning the mind and equipping the mind.
There are eight types of rebirth resulting from giving.
Here, friends, a certain person gives a gift—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps—to a recluse or a brahmin.
Thus, he gives while expecting something in return.
He sees a wealthy kshatriya, a wealthy brahmin, or a wealthy householder endowed with and enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It occurs to him:
‘Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of wealthy khattiyas, or wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders!
He fixes his mind on this, resolves upon it, and develops that thought. That thought of his—liberated from the inferior and not developed further—leads to rebirth there.
And I say this applies to one who is virtuous, not to one who is immoral.
“Friends, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
Furthermore, friends, here someone gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food and drink, and so forth, up to bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
Whatever he gives, that he expects in return.”
He has heard:
"The gods of the Four Great Kings are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness.
It occurs to him:
‘Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings!
He fixes his mind on this, resolves upon it, and develops it. That mind of his—liberated from the inferior and not developed further—leads to rebirth there.
And I say this is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
"The mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds, friends, because of its purity.
Furthermore, friends, here someone gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food and drink... [and so on] ...bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
What he gives, that he expects in return."
He has heard:
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods … the Yāma gods …” [and so forth].
"The Tusita devas...
the Nimmānaratī devas...
the Paranimmitavasavattī devas are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness."
It occurs to him:
“Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas!
He fixes his mind on that, resolves upon that, and develops that mind. Since that mind is liberated from the inferior and not developed further, it leads to rebirth there.
And that, I say, belongs to the virtuous one, not to the immoral one.
For, friends, the mental aspiration of the virtuous one succeeds because of its purity.
Furthermore, friends, here someone gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
Thus, what he gives, that he expects in return. He has heard:
"The deities of Brahma’s retinue are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness."
It occurs to him:
"O, that upon the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of the Brahmakāyika devas!
He fixes his mind on that, resolves upon that, and develops that mind. Since that mind is liberated from what is inferior and not further developed, it leads to rebirth there.
And that, friends, I say is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral;
for one who is free from lust, not for one who still has lust.
For the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of his freedom from lust.
The eight assemblies:

the assembly of kshatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
The eight worldly conditions:
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
The eight bases of mastery:
One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see."
This is the first base of mastery.
Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is how one has such a perception.
This is the second sphere of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the third sphere of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Just as the flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;
or just as that Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;

even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster. Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see."
This is the fifth base of mastery.

Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster—just as, for example, a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster; just as...
Or again, just as there might be a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster;

even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster, and having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as a *bandhujīvaka* flower is red, red in color, red in appearance,
and red in luster, or like a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, which is red, red in color, [red in appearance, and red in luster].
Red in appearance, red in luster;

even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are red, red-colored, red in appearance, and red in luster. Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance,
and white in luster— just like the morning star Osadhī, which is white, white in color,
white in appearance, and white in luster, or like a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.

In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white in appearance, and white in luster; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery.
These are the eight liberations.
Possessing form, one sees forms.
This is the first liberation.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally.
This is the second liberation.
He is intent upon the beautiful alone;
this is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation.
Having completely surmounted the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the eighth liberation.
These, friends, are the eight things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together in harmony... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
9. The Ninefold Set:
"Friends, there are nine things that have been rightly expounded by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
in these, all should recite together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans."
Which nine?
The nine grounds for resentment:
“He has done me harm,” one harbors resentment;
‘He has acted for my harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He will act for my harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me,’ one harbors resentment … [and so on] …
“He has acted for my harm,” he harbors resentment;
“… he is acting for my harm,” he harbors resentment; “… he will act for my harm,” he harbors resentment;
“He has acted for the benefit of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me,” he harbors resentment; [and so on] …
"One binds resentment thinking, 'He has done me harm'...
one binds resentment thinking, 'He will do me harm.
There are nine ways of removing resentment."
‘He has done me harm; how could that be otherwise?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He is doing me harm; how could that be otherwise?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He will do me harm; how could that be otherwise?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me… he is acting for their harm… he will act for their harm; how could this be?’— in this way, one dispels resentment.
‘He acted for the welfare of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me...
he acts for their welfare...
he will act for their welfare; how could this be otherwise?’—in this way, he dispels resentment.
The nine abodes of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first abode of beings.
"There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who were first reborn there.
This is the second abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods."
This is the third abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.
This is the fourth abode of beings.
"Friends, there are beings who are non-percipient and devoid of experience, such as the Non-percipient Devas.
This is the fifth abode of beings.

Friends, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' have reached the sphere of infinite space."
This is the sixth abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the seventh abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the eighth abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the ninth abode of beings.
There are nine inopportune times, non-seasons for living the holy life.

Here, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha; and the Dhamma is taught—leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata.
And this person is reborn in hell.
This is the first inopportune moment, the unfavorable time for living the holy life.

Furthermore, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is being taught—leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata.
And this person is reborn in the animal realm.
This is the second inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore... [as before]...
He is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
This is the third inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore... [and so on]...
He is reborn in the company of the asuras.
This is the fourth inopportune and untimely occasion for leading the holy life.
Furthermore... [and so on] ...
He is reborn in some long-lived order of devas.
This is the fifth inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore... [and so on]...
He is reborn in a remote border region among the barbarians who do not understand [the Dhamma], where there is no access for monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen.
This is the sixth inopportune moment, the wrong time, for living the holy life.
Furthermore... [and so on]...
He is reborn in the central provinces. Yet he holds wrong view and possesses perverted vision:
"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world, there is no mother, there is no father, and there are no beings..."

‘Beings are spontaneously born; there are no recluses or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
This is the seventh inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore, ...
he is reborn in the Middle Countries; yet he is dull-witted, stupid, and mute, incapable of discerning the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This is the eighth inopportune moment, the wrong time for leading the holy life.
Furthermore, friends, when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One has not appeared in the world,
and the Dhamma— conducive to peace, conducive to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, and proclaimed by the Sugata— is not being taught;
and yet this person is reborn in the Middle Countries, and he is wise, not dull-witted, and not deaf-mute.
He is capable of discerning the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This is the ninth inopportune moment, the non-season for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
The nine successive dwellings (*anupubbavihāra*).

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
With the fading away as well of rapture... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna."
With the abandoning of pleasure … [and so on] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form … [and so on] … he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
By completely surmounting the base of infinite space, perceiving that "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
There are nine successive cessations.
For one who has attained the first jhāna, sensual perceptions have ceased.
For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought and sustained thought have ceased.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased.
For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, inhalation and exhalation have ceased.
For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has ceased.
For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has ceased.
For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased.
For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased.
These, friends, are the nine things that have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In this regard, all should recite them together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
10. The Decade:
There are, friends, ten things that have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Which ten?
The ten qualities that make one a protector.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
This, too, is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is learned, a bearer of the heard, a storehouse of the heard—those teachings which...
They proclaim a holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, both in meaning and in phrasing; they are entirely complete and pure.
Such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well penetrated through right view.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is learned … [as above] … with a view well-penetrated.
This quality, too, is a source of protection.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
Furthermore, friends, that a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates—
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is easy to correct, endowed with qualities that make him easy to correct, patient, and receptive to instruction.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is easy to speak to... [as above] ...and he receives instruction respectfully.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is skillful and diligent regarding those various duties for his fellow celibates, both major and minor; he possesses the necessary ingenuity to carry them out and to organize them effectively.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu [is able] to provide for his fellow celibates...
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who loves the Dhamma, who delights in its proclamation, and who finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is one who loves the Dhamma... [and so on] ...he has a sublime joy.
This too is a quality that makes for a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites he receives.
This, too, is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states.
This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recalls what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago. This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is mindful... [as above] ...one who remembers and recollects.
This too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is wise ... [as above] ... leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
This too is a quality that provides a protector.
The ten kasiṇa bases.
One person perceives the earth-kasina, above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable.
One person perceives the water-kasina … one person perceives the fire-kasina … [and so on].
One person perceives the air kasiṇa;
another perceives the blue kasiṇa;
another perceives the yellow kasiṇa.
One perceives the red kasiṇa...
one perceives the white kasiṇa...
one perceives the space kasiṇa...
One perceives the consciousness-kasina above, below, and across, non-dual and immeasurable.
The ten unwholesome courses of action:
killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
The ten courses of wholesome action: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct,
abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, and non-covetousness.
Non-ill will and right view.
The ten noble abodes.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, and has four supports.
One who has shaken off individual dogmatic views, who has completely abandoned seeking, whose intentions are undisturbed, whose bodily formations are tranquilized,
and who is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned five factors?
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, abandoned ill will, abandoned sloth and torpor, abandoned restlessness and remorse, and abandoned doubt.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu possessed of six factors?"
"Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending."
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with six factors.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has a single guard?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness.
"In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has a single guard.
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have a fourfold support?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures one thing; having reflected, he avoids one thing; and having reflected, he dispels one thing."
"In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has four supports.
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have shaken off his individual truths?
Here, friends, whatever various individual truths held by various recluses and brahmins—all those are shaken off, dispelled, abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and discarded."
"In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has shaken off individual dogmatic views.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has utterly abandoned seeking?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned the seeking for sensual pleasures, he has abandoned the seeking for existence, and the seeking for a holy life has subsided."
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has thoroughly relinquished his search.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose intentions are undisturbed?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned thoughts of sensual desire, abandoned thoughts of ill will, and abandoned thoughts of cruelty.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu is one whose intentions are undisturbed.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose bodily formations have been stilled?

Here, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has tranquilized the bodily formations.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in mind?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu is one whose mind is well-liberated.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose wisdom is well-liberated?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu understands: "Lust has been abandoned by me; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising."
‘Hatred has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future,’ he understands.
‘Delusion has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future,’ he understands.
It is in this way, friend, that a bhikkhu is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.

The ten qualities of one beyond training: the right view of one beyond training, the right intention of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training,

the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, the right concentration of one beyond training, [the right knowledge, and the right liberation].
The final right knowledge of one beyond training, and the final right liberation of one beyond training.
These, friends, are the ten things that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding these, all should recite them together and not dispute them, so that this holy life may endure for a long time.
"May it endure for long; may it be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Then the Blessed One rose and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is well that you have spoken this method for the communal recitation of the monks.
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said, and the Teacher approved.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Saṅgītisutta, the tenth, is finished.
